mainTopic: The source for יהרג ואל יעבור in רציחה (a סברא from רבא), followed by stories about an עוברה who smelled food on יום כיפור
overview: Earlier, the גמרא learned that גילוי עריות falls under יהרג ואל יעבור by comparing it to רציחה. Now it asks how we know this rule for רציחה itself. The answer is a סברא, shown through a story: a man came to רבא and said the ruler of his town had ordered him to kill someone or be killed. רבא told him to let himself be killed rather than kill, because who says your blood is redder than his? The גמרא then turns back to the משנה's case of an עוברה who smelled food on יום כיפור and craved it. In the first story, רבי told people to whisper to her that it was יום כיפור. It worked, and her baby grew up to be רבי יוחנן. In the second story, רבי חנינא gave the same advice, but it did not work. The amud ends as רבי חנינא begins to quote a פסוק about that baby, and the פסוק comes on the next amud.

steps.title: What is the source for the murderer himself?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know that a person must let himself be killed rather than commit רציחה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for the murderer himself, how do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source of the rule about רציחה itself. This question sets up the next step, which gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, גילוי עריות was compared to רציחה, so it borrowed the rule of יהרג ואל יעבור from רציחה. But that comparison only works if we already know the rule for רציחה. So the גמרא now asks where the rule for רציחה comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: How do we know this? (asking for a source)

phrases.english: And the murderer himself
phrases.notes: Meaning the main case of murder, which other cases were compared to.

phrases.english: from where do we know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the base case that the earlier comparison to גילוי עריות depended on.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for the rule that one must die rather than commit רציחה.

steps.title: It is logic: the case brought before רבא
steps.stepSummary: The answer is that the rule comes from a סברא, not from a פסוק. A story with רבא shows this: a man was ordered to kill someone or be killed himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is logical reasoning. For example, a man came before רבא and said: 'The ruler of my town told me: Kill so-and-so, and if you don't, I will kill you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the rule is based on a סברא. It begins a story with רבא that will show the reasoning, and the next step gives רבא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually the גמרא looks for a פסוק as a source. Here it says that plain logic is enough. The case is a direct choice: your life or someone else's. That is exactly the situation the rule is about.

keyTerms.meaning: the master or ruler of my town

steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for a פסוק here. The גמרא is saying the rule for רציחה comes from logic alone, and a סברא carries real legal weight.

phrases.english: It is logical reasoning:
as a certain man came before Rava,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, אֲמַר לִי מָרֵי דּוּרַאי:
phrases.english: he said to him: The master of my village said to me:
Kill so-and-so,
and if not, I will kill you.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source is a סברא, shown through a case brought before רבא.

steps.title: רבא: Who says your blood is redder?
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that the man must let himself be killed and must not kill. His reason: nobody can say his own life is worth more than someone else's.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא told him: Let them kill you, and do not kill. Why do you think your blood is redder? Maybe that other man's blood is redder!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his ruling and the reasoning behind it. This reasoning is the סברא the גמרא promised in the previous step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally פיקוח נפש lets you break a rule to save your life. Here, though, you would be saving your life by ending another life. Since no one can show that his life matters more, the reason to break the rule falls away, and you may not kill.

keyTerms.meaning: Let them kill you, and do not kill

steps.whatToRemember: רציחה is יהרג ואל יעבור because of a סברא: one life cannot be traded for another, since no one knows whose blood is redder.
steps.whyThisMatters: This סברא is the base for the whole idea of יהרג ואל יעבור in רציחה. גילוי עריות gets its rule from here too.

phrases.english: He said to him: Let him kill you, and do not kill.
What did you see
that your blood is redder?
Perhaps the blood of that man
is redder!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי חָזֵית דִּדְמָא דִּידָךְ סוּמָּק טְפֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story and spells out the סברא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: One may not kill another person to save himself, because his blood is not known to be redder.

steps.title: רבי tells them to whisper to the pregnant woman
steps.stepSummary: An עוברה smelled food on יום כיפור and craved it. רבי said to whisper to her that it was יום כיפור. It worked, and her baby became רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: A pregnant woman smelled food. They came to רבי. He said: Go whisper to her that today is יום כיפור. They whispered, and it worked. He applied to the baby the פסוק: 'Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you.' רבי יוחנן was born from her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה's case of an עוברה who craves food. It tells a story showing a first step to try before feeding her: remind her that it is יום כיפור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה allows feeding her. This story shows that a gentle reminder may calm the craving, so she does not need to eat at all. Because the reminder worked, the baby was seen as holy even before birth.

keyTerms.meaning: she was affected by the whisper (it worked)
came out of her (was born from her)

phrases.english: A certain pregnant woman smelled food,
they came before Rabbi,
he said to them: Go whisper to her
that it is Yom Kippur.
They whispered to her and she accepted the whisper.
He read about him:
"Before I formed you in the belly I knew you, etc."
Rabbi Yochanan came out of her.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהִיא עוּבָּרָה דְּאָרַחָא, אֲתוֹ לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of רציחה and goes back to the משנה's case of the עוברה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: First try whispering to her that it is יום כיפור. Then see whether the craving passes.

steps.title: רבי חנינא: the whisper did not work
steps.stepSummary: In a second case, רבי חנינא also said to whisper to the woman, but it did not work. He then begins to quote a פסוק about that baby.
steps.simpleTranslation: A pregnant woman smelled food. They came to רבי חנינא. He said: Whisper to her. But it did not work. He applied to the baby:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story that is the opposite of the first: the whisper failed. The amud ends just before the פסוק, which comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Put next to the first story, this shows that whispering does not always work. When it fails, she would be fed, as the משנה says. רבי חנינא's פסוק, coming next, will reflect how this baby turned out.

keyTerms.meaning: and she was not affected by the whisper
he applied a פסוק to him

phrases.english: A certain pregnant woman smelled food,
they came before Rabbi Chanina.
He said to them: Whisper to her,
but she did not accept the whisper.
He read about him:
phrases.notes: The פסוק comes on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהִיא עוּבָּרָה דְּאָרַחָא, אֲתוֹ לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A matching story with the opposite result.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whispering does not always work. Here it failed.
